headings.title: Introduction to Human Genetics and DNA Structure
headings.content:
Human genetics is the study of inherited variation in human beings. At the core of this science is **deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA)**, the hereditary material found in almost all human cells. DNA takes the shape of a **double helix**, resembling a twisted ladder. The sides of this ladder consist of alternating sugar and phosphate molecules, while the rungs are formed by pairs of nitrogenous bases.

There are four nitrogenous bases in DNA:
- **Adenine (A)** always pairs with **Thymine (T)**
- **Cytosine (C)** always pairs with **Guanine (G)**

This specific pairing rule is known as complementary base pairing. A sequence of these bases forms the genetic code, instructing the body on how to build proteins necessary for structure, function, and regulation of the body's tissues and organs.

headings.title: Chromosomes, Genes, and the Human Genome
headings.content:
Inside the nucleus of a human cell, DNA is tightly packed into structures called **chromosomes**. Normal somatic human cells contain **46 chromosomes**, arranged in 23 pairs. One set of 23 comes from the mother via the oocyte, and the other set of 23 comes from the father via the sperm. Of these pairs, 22 are **autosomes**, and one pair consists of the **sex chromosomes** (XX for females, XY for males).

A **gene** is a specific segment of DNA located on a chromosome that codes for a particular protein. The entire set of genetic instructions found in a human cell is called the **genome**. While all cells in the human body contain the exact same genome, different cell types activate different genes, allowing skin cells to look and act differently from neurons.

headings.title: Mendelian Inheritance and Punnett Squares
headings.content:
Gregor Mendel discovered the fundamental laws of inheritance using pea plants, which apply to humans as well. Traits are determined by **alleles**, which are alternative forms of a gene. An individual inherits two alleles for each gene, one from each parent.

- **Homozygous**: Having two identical alleles for a specific trait (e.g., TT or tt).
- **Heterozygous**: Having two different alleles for a specific trait (e.g., Tt).
- **Dominant allele**: Expressed even when only one copy is present (represented by a capital letter).
- **Recessive allele**: Expressed only when two copies are present (represented by a lowercase letter).

A **Punnett square** is a simple grid tool nurses and geneticists use to predict the probability of an offspring inheriting a particular genotype or phenotype based on parental alleles.

headings.title: Non-Mendelian Inheritance Patterns
headings.content:
Not all human traits follow strict dominant and recessive rules. Complex human characteristics often involve varied interaction types.

- **Incomplete dominance**: The heterozygous phenotype is an intermediate blend between the two homozygous variants (e.g., red and white flowers producing pink).
- **Codominance**: Both alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed without blending, such as the AB blood group where A and B antigens appear together on red blood cells.
- **Polygenic inheritance**: Multiple genes combine to influence a single phenotypic trait, such as height, skin color, or eye color.
- **X-linked inheritance**: Genes located on the X chromosome show distinct inheritance patterns because males carry only one X chromosome and express any allele found on it, whether dominant or recessive.

headings.title: Chromosomal Abnormalities and Mutations
headings.content:
Changes in genetic material can happen at the molecular level or the chromosomal level. A **mutation** is a permanent alteration in the DNA sequence. Mutations can be point mutations (changes in a single nucleotide base) or frameshift mutations (insertion or deletion of nucleotides that shifts the reading frame).

At the cellular level, **nondisjunction** is a major source of chromosomal abnormalities. This occurs when homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids fail to separate properly during meiosis. Nondisjunction results in **aneuploidy**, an abnormal number of chromosomes, such as **monosony** (missing a chromosome) or **trisomy** (having an extra chromosome, like in Down syndrome).

headings.title: Common Genetic Disorders in Clinical Practice
headings.content:
Nurses frequently encounter patients managing inherited or congenital conditions. Understanding their transmission patterns is critical for safe clinical care.

- **Sickle Cell Anemia**: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by a point mutation in the hemoglobin gene, leading to abnormal sickled red blood cells that block small blood vessels.
- **Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)**: Caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, characterized by intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, and congenital heart defects.
- **Hemophilia A**: An X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency in clotting factor VIII, leading to prolonged bleeding times.
- **Cystic Fibrosis**: An autosomal recessive condition affecting chloride channels, resulting in thick, sticky mucus buildup in the lungs and digestive tract.

headings.title: Genetic Counseling and Nursing Assessment
headings.content:
Nurses play a vital role in identifying patients at risk for genetic conditions and providing compassionate support. A comprehensive **genogram** (family pedigree) is an essential assessment tool used to map inherited diseases across three or more generations.

Genetic counseling helps families understand diagnoses, recurrence risks, and testing options. Nurses assist by taking thorough family histories, identifying red flags such as early-onset cancer or multiple miscarriages, and offering emotional support while maintaining patient confidentiality and autonomy in decision-making.
